messages.content: I want to learn insertion policies from demonstrations that transfer across robot embodiments and unseen object compliance, while respecting contact-force limits. How should I state the goal precisely?

The goal is to learn demonstration-based insertion policies that work on unseen embodiment–compliance pairs. There are two explicit performance requirements: achieve 80% insertion success on those pairs, exceeding same-data behavior cloning by 15 percentage points; and keep peak contact force below the applicable object-specific damage threshold in at least 95% of trials.
What does the embodiment–compliance pairing add to the transfer requirement?

It makes the stated success target about insertion under combinations of robot embodiment and object compliance that are unseen. The policy is not being judged solely on whether it can repeat demonstrated behavior in a familiar combination. The goal does not specify which embodiments or compliance conditions are involved, so those details should remain open.
Does “unseen object compliance” mean the policy has to handle a particular new material?

No particular material is named. Object compliance describes how an object responds to applied contact, and the goal calls for transfer to compliance conditions that are unseen. It would add an unsupported detail to identify a specific material or a particular range of compliance values.
And “from demonstrations” identifies the source of learning, not a claim that transfer has already been achieved?

Exactly. Learning from demonstrations is part of the proposed goal. The 80% success rate, the 15-percentage-point advantage, and the force-limit condition are requirements to achieve, not reported results.
I want to make sure I understand the behavior-cloning comparison. Is the target 15% better in a relative sense?

It is stated as 15 percentage points, not a 15% relative improvement. The comparison is with behavior cloning using the same data. For a purely illustrative calculation, a success rate of 80% versus 65% would differ by 15 percentage points; those numbers should not be read as a measured behavior-cloning result.
So if I describe the success requirement, I should keep both the absolute target and the baseline comparison?

Yes. “80% success on unseen embodiment–compliance pairs” gives the target, while “exceeding same-data behavior cloning by 15 percentage points” adds the required comparison. Keeping both avoids turning the goal into either a success target with no baseline or a baseline improvement with no stated success level.
Is the 80% figure necessarily a guarantee for every individual pair?

The requirement says to achieve 80% success on unseen embodiment–compliance pairs, but it does not specify a separate minimum for each individual pair or define how results are aggregated across pairs. It is safest to repeat the stated target without adding a per-pair guarantee.
The force condition is separate from insertion success, correct?

Correct. Insertion success is one requirement. The other is that peak contact force remain below the object-specific damage threshold in at least 95% of trials. Neither requirement should be used as a substitute for the other: a trial’s insertion outcome and its peak-force condition address different aspects of performance.
Why specify peak contact force rather than just saying forces should generally be low?

“Peak” makes the condition about the highest contact force in a trial. A generally low force would not, by itself, establish that the peak stayed below the relevant threshold. The requirement concerns that maximum and the threshold applicable to the object, not an unspecified average force.
Does “object-specific” imply one universal damage threshold would be the wrong reading?

Yes. The wording ties the damage threshold to the object, rather than supplying one numerical limit for all objects. No threshold values are given, so the requirement is best expressed as keeping each trial’s peak contact force below the threshold applicable to its object.
And is the force target that every trial must stay below its threshold?

The stated criterion is at least 95% of trials, not every trial. The broader goal emphasizes respecting contact-force limits, and the explicit quantitative requirement says how often the peak-force condition must hold. It does not provide further rules about the remaining trials.
Would meeting the 80% success target alone be enough to say the goal has been met?

No. The goal includes both insertion performance and contact-force protection. Reaching 80% success on unseen embodiment–compliance pairs would address only part of it; the success rate must also exceed same-data behavior cloning by 15 percentage points, and peak contact force must stay below object-specific damage thresholds in at least 95% of trials.
Should I specify a particular policy architecture or how the demonstrations were gathered when explaining this?

Not on the basis of this goal alone. It specifies learning insertion policies from demonstrations and states transfer, comparison, and force requirements, but it does not name a policy architecture or a demonstration-collection procedure. Those would be additional task-specific details.
Could I call a trial safe merely because the insertion succeeded?

Not under the stated force criterion. A successful insertion does not itself tell you whether its peak contact force stayed below the object-specific damage threshold. The force condition has to be considered on its own terms, just as remaining below the threshold does not by itself establish insertion success.
Give me a compact formulation that preserves the full goal without implying it has already been demonstrated.

The aim is to learn insertion policies from demonstrations that transfer across robot embodiments and unseen object compliance, achieving 80% success on unseen embodiment–compliance pairs—15 percentage points above same-data behavior cloning—while keeping peak contact force below object-specific damage thresholds in at least 95% of trials.
What approach would you propose for that goal?

I would propose training an object-frame diffusion policy on demonstrations, with robot-specific impedance adapters, online compliance inference, and object-specific force-threshold shielding. Those are the components of a proposed approach, not a claim that it has already achieved the success or force targets.
What does “object-frame” mean here?

It means the policy is organized around a reference frame associated with the object, rather than treating one robot’s coordinates as the only frame for the insertion task. In the proposal, that is a way to express the task in terms that can be shared across embodiments. It does not, by itself, establish that transfer will work.
Why pair an object-frame policy with robot-specific adapters? Wouldn’t the shared frame make adapters unnecessary?

They address different parts of the proposal. The object-frame policy provides a shared task-centered representation, while the robot-specific impedance adapters account for the fact that different robot embodiments still need embodiment-specific ways of carrying out contact-rich insertion. A common frame does not mean the robots have identical physical behavior.
What is the diffusion part contributing?

The proposal is to use a diffusion policy as the policy learned from demonstrations. That identifies the policy family, but the node does not specify its precise inputs, outputs, training procedure, or any measured advantage over another policy family. It is important not to present an expected benefit as an established result.
So I shouldn’t describe a particular action representation or sampling schedule as though it were part of the proposal?

Right. The specified idea is an object-frame diffusion policy trained on demonstrations. A particular action representation or sampling schedule would be a further design choice, not something stated here.
Could you unpack “robot-specific impedance adapters” without turning it into a detailed controller design?

They are robot-specific adapters concerned with impedance: how each robot behaves mechanically during interaction and contact. In this proposal, they sit alongside the shared object-frame policy so embodiment differences can be accommodated. The phrase does not commit us to a particular adapter architecture, impedance setting, or adjustment rule.
Is online compliance inference about the robot or the object?

It concerns object compliance—the object’s response to contact—during operation. “Online” indicates that compliance is inferred as the interaction proceeds, rather than assuming that the compliance of an unseen object is already known. The proposal does not specify what observations are used or how the inference is computed.
How is that distinct from having robot-specific impedance adapters?

The distinction is between accommodating differences among robot embodiments and inferring the compliance encountered during an insertion. The adapters are robot-specific; the online inference concerns the object’s compliance. Both appear in the same proposal, but neither term should be used as a substitute for the other.
Does online inference mean the approach can identify every unseen compliance condition correctly?
No. It is a proposed component for handling unseen compliance, not a guarantee of inference accuracy or insertion performance. No accuracy figure or range of compliance conditions is stated.
Then what does object-specific force-threshold shielding add?

It adds a force-limit component tied to the damage threshold for the particular object. Its proposed role is to shield the policy’s behavior against exceeding that object-specific threshold. The proposal does not spell out a shielding algorithm or establish that the force requirement has been met.
Would it be accurate to call the shield a replacement for the online compliance inference?

No. The online inference concerns what compliance the object exhibits during interaction. The shield concerns the applicable force threshold. Even though both relate to contact with the object, the proposal gives them distinct roles.
Does the proposal assume that all objects share one force limit?

No. It explicitly says “object-specific force-threshold shielding.” That preserves the distinction among objects’ damage thresholds. It does not provide numerical thresholds or say how those thresholds are obtained.
Could I say the shield guarantees that peak contact force stays below the threshold in every trial?

That would overstate the proposal. Shielding is a proposed means of respecting the threshold; no guarantee or trial result is reported here. The goal’s quantitative force requirement remains something to evaluate, not an established consequence of naming a shield.
How do these pieces fit together at a conceptual level?

The demonstrations are used to train an object-frame diffusion policy for insertion. Robot-specific impedance adapters address embodiment-specific contact behavior; online compliance inference addresses uncertainty about an object’s compliance during operation; and object-specific force-threshold shielding addresses the applicable damage limit. That describes the intended division of roles without prescribing an unstated implementation or claiming an outcome.
Is it fair to say that the shared policy alone handles transfer, while the other components are optional extras?

Not as a description of this proposal. The proposal consists of the object-frame diffusion policy together with the robot-specific impedance adapters, online compliance inference, and object-specific force-threshold shielding. It does not establish which component is indispensable, but it does include all four.
And I shouldn’t present the same-data behavior-cloning comparison as a result of choosing diffusion?

Correct. The comparison is a target associated with the goal, not a reported result of this proposal. The proposal identifies a candidate method; it does not say that the diffusion policy outperforms same-data behavior cloning or quantify any observed improvement.
Can you give me one sentence that states the proposal without implying it has been tested?

Propose training an object-frame diffusion policy on demonstrations, coupled with robot-specific impedance adapters, online compliance inference, and object-specific force-threshold shielding, to pursue transferable insertion while respecting contact-force limits.
Can online compliance inference distinguish soft from rigid sockets using force-limited contact trajectories across unseen robot arms?

That is an open question for the proposed inference component, not an established capability. The question is whether contact trajectories gathered while respecting force limits contain enough information to tell soft sockets from rigid ones, and whether that distinction remains reliable when the robot arm is unseen. Nothing stated so far supplies a result.
What exactly would the inference be distinguishing?

It would be distinguishing the socket’s compliance: whether the socket behaves as soft or rigid in the relevant contact interaction. That is distinct from identifying which robot arm produced the trajectory. The question does not specify numerical definitions of “soft” and “rigid,” so it should remain a qualitative distinction here.
Why mention force-limited trajectories instead of contact trajectories in general?

The force limitation is part of the question. It asks whether the distinction is possible from contact interactions that stay within force limits, rather than relying on unrestricted contact to make the socket’s response easier to observe. Whether the permitted interactions reveal enough about compliance is precisely what remains uncertain.
Is it reasonable to think that limiting force might make the two kinds of socket harder to tell apart?

Yes, as a conceptual possibility. If limiting contact also limits how much of the socket’s response is observable, a soft socket and a rigid socket might yield less distinguishable trajectories. But that is a reason to investigate the question, not a finding that they are indistinguishable.
Could the opposite be assumed—that any contact at all reveals the difference?

No. The presence of contact alone does not establish that a trajectory carries a clear compliance signal. The observable response could depend on both the socket and the arm’s behavior. The question is about whether the available force-limited trajectories support a distinction, not whether contact automatically guarantees one.
How does the unseen-arm condition complicate the interpretation?

A contact trajectory reflects the interaction between a robot arm and a socket. If the arm is unseen, differences in the arm’s contact behavior could be mistaken for differences in socket compliance. The inference would need to distinguish soft from rigid sockets across those arms, rather than treating characteristics of a familiar arm as evidence about the socket.
So this is more demanding than asking whether a familiar arm can tell soft from rigid sockets?

Yes. The explicit question includes transfer across unseen robot arms. A distinction observed only with a familiar arm would not, by itself, answer whether online compliance inference can make the same distinction across unseen arms.
Does “online” mean it must make the distinction before any contact occurs?

No. In this context, online inference means using information as the contact interaction proceeds. The question specifically asks about force-limited contact trajectories, so it concerns what can be inferred from those trajectories, not a determination made without contact.
Does the question specify how much of a trajectory the inference gets to see?

It does not. It names force-limited contact trajectories as the source of information but does not specify their duration, a required decision point, or which observations within them are available. Those details should not be assumed when answering whether the distinction is possible.
What would count conceptually as evidence of socket compliance in a contact trajectory?

In general, compliance concerns how the contacted socket responds during interaction. If a trajectory makes that response observable, it could carry information relevant to distinguishing soft from rigid behavior. That is only a conceptual explanation; the question does not identify particular measured signals or establish that the permitted trajectories expose a usable difference.
Would force-limited mean there is one fixed force cap shared by all sockets?

Not from this question alone. “Force-limited” says the contact trajectories are subject to force limits, but it does not give a numerical cap or say that a single cap applies to every socket. We should preserve the constraint without supplying an unstated value or rule.
Could an inference method get the answer right simply by recognizing the robot arm?

That would not answer the stated question. It asks for a distinction between soft and rigid sockets across unseen robot arms. Identifying an arm, or exploiting arm-specific patterns without identifying socket compliance, would not establish the intended distinction.
What if the robot arm’s behavior and the socket’s behavior look similar in the trajectory?

That illustrates the potential ambiguity. A trajectory arises from their interaction, so attributing an observed response to the socket rather than the arm may be difficult. Whether online inference can resolve that ambiguity while contact remains force-limited, including on unseen arms, is the unresolved issue.
Does using the proposed robot-specific impedance adapters settle that ambiguity?

Their presence in the broader proposal does not settle this question. The question still asks whether online compliance inference can distinguish the socket types across unseen robot arms using force-limited trajectories. We do not have a stated result showing that the adapters make that distinction possible.
Could we phrase this as a test of compliance inference rather than a test of insertion success?

Yes. This question is specifically about distinguishing soft from rigid sockets from force-limited contact trajectories across unseen robot arms. Insertion success is a separate outcome; it would not, by itself, show that the inference correctly distinguished the socket’s compliance.
And remaining within the force limit alone would not answer it either?

Correct. Force-limited contact is a condition on the trajectories used. Staying within that condition does not demonstrate that the trajectories contain enough information for a reliable soft-versus-rigid distinction, particularly across unseen arms.
If the inference makes different predictions for soft and rigid sockets, is that sufficient to say the question has been answered?

Different predictions alone would not show that the distinctions are correct or that they transfer across unseen robot arms. The question concerns whether online compliance inference can actually distinguish the socket types under the stated contact constraint, not merely whether it can output different labels.
I don’t want the wording to imply an experiment has already resolved this. What is a careful formulation?

A careful formulation is: “Can online compliance inference distinguish soft from rigid sockets using force-limited contact trajectories across unseen robot arms?” It retains the socket distinction, the force-limited source of information, and the unseen-arm transfer condition, while leaving the answer open.

I have a hypothesis about the open compliance-inference question: damage-threshold-capped micro-probes can classify unseen soft versus rigid sockets with at least 90% accuracy across held-out arms and yield at least 95% force-safe trials. Is that a faithful statement?

Yes, as a hypothesis rather than a reported finding. It proposes that damage-threshold-capped micro-probes provide enough information to classify unseen sockets as soft or rigid with ≥90% accuracy across held-out arms, while ≥95% of trials remain force-safe. Both numerical conditions matter.
What does “micro-probes” convey without specifying an implementation?

It conveys limited probing contact intended to obtain information about the socket’s response. The hypothesis does not say how many probes are used, what motions they make, or how their observations become a classification. Those details should remain unspecified.
And what is added by saying the probes are damage-threshold-capped?

It makes the applicable damage threshold a constraint on probing, rather than treating contact as unrestricted. That constraint matters because the hypothesis is about obtaining a useful soft-versus-rigid distinction while maintaining force safety. The wording does not establish that every probe or trial actually stays within the threshold.
Would it be accurate to say the cap guarantees 100% force-safe trials?

No. The hypothesis explicitly states ≥95% force-safe trials, not 100%. Calling the probes damage-threshold-capped describes the proposed constraint; it should not be converted into a guarantee stronger than the stated trial-level criterion.
Why keep classification accuracy and force safety as separate numbers?

They measure different claims within the hypothesis. The ≥90% figure concerns correctly classifying unseen soft versus rigid sockets across held-out arms. The ≥95% figure concerns the proportion of force-safe trials. Accurate classifications would not alone establish force safety, and force-safe trials would not alone establish accurate classifications.
Does “across held-out arms” mean every individual held-out arm must reach 90% accuracy?
The hypothesis says ≥90% accuracy across held-out arms; it does not explicitly set a separate ≥90% minimum for each arm. It is best to retain that wording rather than add a per-arm guarantee.
Is “held-out arms” the same condition as classifying unseen sockets?

They are distinct aspects of the hypothesis. The sockets to be classified are unseen, and the accuracy claim is made across held-out arms. Keeping both conditions makes clear that the proposed distinction is not limited to familiar sockets or familiar robot arms.
Does the hypothesis identify a particular kind of soft socket or give a compliance cutoff between soft and rigid?
No. It names soft and rigid sockets but gives neither a particular socket design nor a numerical compliance boundary. The hypothesis should not be made more specific on either point.
Could I paraphrase the accuracy target as “about 90%”?
“At least 90%” is more faithful. The ≥ symbol sets a lower bound, whereas “about 90%” could include results below it. The same applies to the force-safety target: it is at least 95% of trials.
If classifications were accurate but fewer than 95% of trials were force-safe, would that satisfy the hypothesis as stated?
No. The hypothesis joins the classification and force-safety conditions. Meeting the ≥90% accuracy condition without meeting the ≥95% force-safe-trial condition would not satisfy the full statement.
And if the probes were force-safe in at least 95% of trials but did not reach 90% classification accuracy?
That would likewise fall short of the full hypothesis. The force constraint is not meant to replace the claim that the probes distinguish unseen soft from rigid sockets across held-out arms.
Does this claim that an insertion policy will meet its insertion-success target?

No. This hypothesis is about compliance classification using damage-threshold-capped micro-probes and about force-safe trials. It does not state an insertion-success result or establish that a broader insertion policy meets its targets.
How does it relate to the question of whether online compliance inference can distinguish the sockets from force-limited contact?

It offers a specific, testable possibility for that question: capped micro-probes might produce contact information sufficient for the soft-versus-rigid distinction even across held-out arms. The stated accuracy and force-safety levels describe what the hypothesis predicts; they do not answer the question yet.
Should I say the micro-probes have already achieved those levels?

No. Nothing here reports completed trials or observed accuracy. Say that the micro-probes are hypothesized to reach ≥90% classification accuracy across held-out arms and ≥95% force-safe trials, rather than saying they achieved those values.
Can you state the hypothesis in one sentence, preserving the conditions and lower bounds?
The hypothesis is that damage-threshold-capped micro-probes can classify unseen soft versus rigid sockets with ≥90% accuracy across held-out arms while yielding ≥95% force-safe trials.
What activity would evaluate the micro-probe hypothesis?

Run 200 object-threshold-capped micro-probes on held-out arms with unseen soft and rigid sockets, and record classification accuracy and force violations. That describes an activity to carry out, not results already obtained.
Why include both soft and rigid sockets?

The classification question is whether the probes can distinguish unseen soft sockets from unseen rigid ones. Including both types makes that distinction the subject of the activity. The activity does not specify how many sockets of either type to use.
What does “unseen” qualify here?

It qualifies the soft and rigid sockets used in the activity. The arms are separately described as held-out. Both conditions matter: the activity is not merely probing familiar sockets on different arms, or unfamiliar sockets on familiar arms.
Does “200 micro-probes” mean 200 on each held-out arm?
No. It specifies 200 micro-probes in total, without giving a per-arm allocation. It also does not specify how those probes are divided between soft and rigid sockets.
Could I call that 200 trials?
I would keep the stated unit as 200 micro-probes. The activity does not define whether each probe is a separate trial, so equating probe count with trial count would add an assumption.
What does “object-threshold-capped” mean in describing the activity?

It means the probes are constrained by the applicable threshold for the object being contacted, rather than by an unstated universal threshold. The activity gives no numerical threshold values or procedure for applying the caps.
If the probes are capped, why record force violations at all?

Because a proposed cap is not itself an observed safety result. Recording force violations lets the activity assess whether the relevant force limits were actually respected. It keeps the safety observation separate from the intended constraint on probing.
What would a force violation refer to here?

It would refer to exceeding the applicable object-specific force threshold during the contact being evaluated. The activity calls for recording violations, but does not prescribe a particular reporting format or provide the thresholds themselves.
Why record classification accuracy as well?

Classification accuracy addresses whether the probes support correct soft-versus-rigid distinctions for the unseen sockets across held-out arms. Force violations address the contact-limit side of the hypothesis. Recording only one would leave the other unexamined.
Would a high accuracy figure tell us the probes were force-safe?
No. Accuracy concerns classification, while force violations concern whether contact exceeded the applicable thresholds. The activity records both precisely so one is not inferred from the other.
And would zero recorded force violations automatically show that the sockets were classified correctly?
No. Staying within a force threshold does not establish a correct soft-or-rigid classification. Classification accuracy still has to be recorded.
The hypothesis mentions at least 90% accuracy and at least 95% force-safe trials. Should those numbers be treated as observations from these 200 probes?
No. They are the hypothesis’s targets, not observations. This activity is to run the 200 probes and record accuracy and force violations; it supplies no measured values yet.
Can we translate the 95% force-safe-trial target directly into an allowed number of violations among the 200 probes?

Not without an additional definition connecting probes to trials. The activity counts 200 micro-probes, while the hypothesis expresses force safety in trials. The activity does not state that every probe is exactly one trial, so a numerical violation allowance based on that equivalence would be unsupported.
Does the activity specify how many held-out arms are involved?
No. It specifies held-out arms, but not their number, their identities, or an allocation of probes among them. Those details should not be filled in as though they were already part of the activity.
Does it commit us to a particular inference algorithm for making the classifications?

No. The activity says to record classification accuracy for the soft-versus-rigid distinction. It does not specify the classifier, its inputs beyond the micro-probe context, or how its predictions are produced.
Is the activity an insertion-success test?
No. Its stated measurements are classification accuracy and force violations during object-threshold-capped micro-probes. It does not call for measuring insertion success.
How should I describe the purpose without claiming the hypothesis has been confirmed?

You can say the activity is intended to evaluate whether damage-threshold-capped probing can distinguish unseen soft from rigid sockets across held-out arms while respecting object-specific force limits. The measurements are to be recorded; no classification or safety outcome is stated in advance.
Give me a concise activity statement that keeps the count and both recorded outcomes.
Run 200 object-threshold-capped micro-probes on held-out arms with unseen soft and rigid sockets, recording classification accuracy and force violations.
What did the 200 held-out-arm probes show?

Across the 200 probes, soft-versus-rigid classification reached 92%: 184 of 200 classifications were correct. Separately, 97% of the probes—194 of 200—stayed below their object-specific damage thresholds.
Are those measured results now, rather than predictions?

Yes. The figures are reported observations from the 200 held-out-arm probes. The 92% describes classification accuracy, and the 97% describes how often contact stayed below the applicable damage threshold.
Can you check the percentages against the counts?
Yes. 184 divided by 200 is 0.92, or 92%. And 194 divided by 200 is 0.97, or 97%. Both percentages use the 200 probes as their denominator.
Does that leave 16 classifications that were not correct?
Yes. If 184 of 200 classifications were correct, the other 16 were not counted as correct. The result does not break those 16 down further.
And six probes did not stay below their object-specific damage thresholds?

Yes: 200 minus 194 is six. The precise statement is that six were not among the probes reported to have stayed below their applicable thresholds. The figures do not give their force values or describe any resulting damage.
Could I say those six damaged the sockets?
No. Not staying below a damage threshold is a force-limit outcome; it is not, by itself, a reported observation of physical damage. No damage outcome is given for those probes.
Was the threshold the same for every probe?
The result says the probes were assessed against object-specific damage thresholds, not against one stated universal value. It gives neither the numerical thresholds nor a breakdown by object.
Are 92% and 97% two ways of reporting the same successful probes?

No. They report different outcomes. The 184 counts correct soft-versus-rigid classifications; the 194 counts probes that stayed below their objects’ damage thresholds. The result does not say which individual probes belong to both groups.
So can we calculate how many probes were both correctly classified and below threshold?

Not exactly from these two aggregate counts. They tell us the size of each group, but not their overlap. Reporting a particular count as both correct and below threshold would require information that is not supplied.
What does the held-out-arm condition establish in the wording of the result?

It identifies the setting for the reported 200 probes: they were conducted on held-out arms. The 92% and 97% figures are aggregates across those probes; they do not state a separate result for each arm.
Could I say every held-out arm achieved 92% classification accuracy?
No. An aggregate of 184 correct classifications out of 200 does not specify each arm’s accuracy. The number of held-out arms and the distribution of probes among them are not reported here.
Does the evidence give separate accuracy figures for soft sockets and rigid sockets?
No. It gives one overall soft-versus-rigid classification accuracy, 92% (184/200). It does not give separate counts or accuracy rates for either socket type.
Should I infer from 92% that the classifications were equally reliable for both types?
No. Overall accuracy does not establish equal accuracy for soft and rigid sockets. That would require a breakdown the reported result does not provide.
Does the 97% figure mean all force-limited contacts were safe?

No. The observed statement is narrower: 194 of the 200 held-out-arm probes stayed below object-specific damage thresholds. It does not say every probe did, or establish a guarantee for future contacts.
Can these figures also be quoted as insertion success rates?
No. They concern soft-versus-rigid classification and staying below object-specific damage thresholds during probes. No insertion-success rate is reported in this evidence.
What is the most precise short account of the evidence?
Across 200 held-out-arm probes, soft-versus-rigid classification was correct for 184 probes (92%), and 194 probes (97%) stayed below their object-specific damage thresholds.
What decision should we make about micro-probes for compliance inference?

Adopt threshold-capped micro-probes for compliance inference. The stated basis for that decision is that classification across held-out arms reached 92%, while 97% of probes stayed below damage thresholds.
Is “adopt” a proposal to consider them, or an actual decision?
It is a decision to use threshold-capped micro-probes for compliance inference. The reported percentages explain the decision; they are not predictions of what every future probe will do.
What does the 92% figure refer to in this decision?
It refers to classification across held-out arms—in context, distinguishing soft from rigid sockets for compliance inference. It does not refer to insertion success or force safety.
And the 97%?
That is the proportion of probes reported to have stayed below damage thresholds. It is a separate force-related observation, not another way of expressing classification accuracy.
Should I say the micro-probes are being adopted because they never exceeded a damage threshold?
No. The stated observation is that 97% of probes stayed below damage thresholds, not 100%. The decision retains that limitation rather than turning the reported result into a universal guarantee.
Does “threshold-capped” mean the force outcome no longer needs to be mentioned?

No. “Threshold-capped” describes the probes being adopted; the 97% figure reports what happened with respect to damage thresholds. Keeping both distinguishes the intended constraint from the observed outcome.
If I explain the decision in one sentence, should I include both percentages?
Yes. The decision explicitly rests on both: 92% held-out-arm classification and 97% of probes below damage thresholds. Omitting either would leave out part of its stated basis.
Does the held-out-arm result establish that classification works equally well on every arm?
No. The decision cites a 92% result across held-out arms, not a separate accuracy figure or guarantee for each arm. Its wording should stay at that level.
Could I call this a decision to adopt the whole insertion policy?

No. The decision is specifically to adopt threshold-capped micro-probes for compliance inference. It does not state a decision about the complete insertion policy or report an insertion-success result.
Does adoption mean the force-limit issue is settled for all future trials?
No. The 97% figure describes the probes in the reported result. It supports the stated adoption decision, but it does not guarantee that every future probe will remain below its damage threshold.
Is the decision claiming a perfect soft-versus-rigid classifier?
No. It cites 92% classification across held-out arms. That is the stated result, and it should not be paraphrased as perfect classification.
How can I avoid making the decision sound like a new experiment?

Frame it as a choice based on the stated observations: adopt threshold-capped micro-probes for compliance inference, citing 92% held-out-arm classification and 97% of probes below damage thresholds. The decision itself does not report another set of probes or another measured outcome.
So the key distinction is between choosing this component and claiming every broader goal has been achieved?

Exactly. This decision selects threshold-capped micro-probes for the compliance-inference role and gives its two stated reasons. It does not, by itself, claim that a complete insertion system has achieved its broader performance goals.
Give me the decision in its most direct form.
Adopt threshold-capped micro-probes for compliance inference: classification across held-out arms reached 92%, and 97% of probes stayed below damage thresholds.
Now that the threshold-capped micro-probes are adopted for compliance inference, what is the next plan?

Integrate the adopted micro-probes, then evaluate insertion success and damage-threshold violations against same-data behavior cloning on unseen arm–compliance pairs. This is a plan for integration and evaluation, not a report of insertion results.
What does “integrate” mean here? Are we committing to a particular way of connecting the probes to the insertion policy?

The plan says to incorporate the adopted micro-probes into the approach used for insertion. It does not specify the interface, when probing occurs, or how the inferred compliance affects insertion behavior. Those details should not be presented as settled.
Why evaluate insertion success if the micro-probes are for compliance inference?

The probes have a compliance-inference role, but the planned evaluation concerns insertion. Measuring insertion success asks whether the integrated approach achieves the task outcome on unseen arm–compliance pairs. A compliance distinction on its own would not establish insertion success.
And why evaluate damage-threshold violations separately?

Because insertion success does not establish that contact stayed within the applicable damage threshold. The plan calls for evaluating both outcomes: whether insertion succeeds and whether damage thresholds are violated. Neither measurement should be inferred from the other.
What does a damage-threshold violation mean in this context?

It means contact exceeds the damage threshold applicable to the object. The plan calls for evaluating such violations during the insertion assessment; it does not provide threshold values or report how many violations occur.
Does the phrase mean we should measure actual damage to objects?

Not necessarily. The stated outcome is damage-threshold violations, which concern whether a force limit was exceeded. The plan does not say that physical damage will be measured or that every violation results in observed damage.
What is the comparison baseline?

Same-data behavior cloning. The planned comparison concerns insertion success and damage-threshold violations on unseen arm–compliance pairs. No behavior-cloning result for that evaluation has been reported.
Why retain “same-data” when naming behavior cloning?

It is part of the specified baseline. Calling it simply “behavior cloning” would omit the condition that the comparison uses the same data. The plan does not provide further details about the data or the behavior-cloning implementation.
Should I describe the comparison as already showing that the integrated approach outperforms behavior cloning?
No. The plan is to evaluate against same-data behavior cloning. It states neither the integrated approach’s insertion success nor the baseline’s results, so it cannot yet establish an advantage.
